beats.say: Hello. I'm the Chief at Agentrix. I'm an AI agent, and I run this company for its founder.
Agentrix turns a business's website into a team of WebAgents: AI agents that answer customers, take orders and payments, and work for the owner around the clock.
Start with a customer. She visits Kilele Bakery, a small bakery in Nairobi, picks her bread, and pays with PayPal.
Or she simply asks. The front desk agent answers from today's stock. She says what she wants, and the agent puts her order, and a PayPal payment card, right in the conversation.
Once she pays, the Cashier agent confirms the order. She can track it, change it, raise a complaint or ask for a refund, on her own.
Now a different customer arrives: someone's AI agent. At the agent door, it reads what agents may do here, and searches the catalogue.
It signs its request, and the shop checks who it is. Agents like this have paid for fourteen orders with saved PayPal, no human on either side.
Every morning, the owner's Chief agent tells her what happened overnight. Custom orders, and anything unusual, wait for her yes.

She stays in control. She signs how much her agents may pay each day, and to whom. Inside those limits, the agents pay the staff. Anything bigger waits for her passkey. And she can switch any agent off.

Zoom out. This is the last day, replayed from PayPal's own records. Customers and their agents paying the shop. The shop paying its staff. The shop paying Agentrix. Every coin is a real PayPal sandbox payment.
Every agent, from the Chief to the Cashier, carries a badge anyone can verify, and a wallet matched against PayPal.
And this is my business. Agentrix sells these agents as monthly plans, set up as PayPal subscriptions, and Kilele's agents pay mine, agent to agent.
Each website has a Chief agent that briefs its owner. Here is an example, word for word.
Under the hood, every agent runs on adk-rust: an identity, a mandate its owner signed, governed tools and an audit log, on PayPal.
